headline: Australia's stagnant productivity since 2020 is raising inflation risk and contributing to frothy domestic valuations
reasoning: Leon argues that Australian labour productivity has gone essentially sideways since 2020, in stark contrast to the US and Japan where productivity has risen materially above trend. He explains that paying workers more without commensurate output gains pushes up costs, which flows into lower profits and higher inflation. This structural productivity gap also partly explains why Australian equity valuations look stretched, and he warns it differentiates Australia negatively from countries investing heavily in technology.
quote: Productivity is ultimately how a country gets wealthier and is measured by calculating how much we produce for every hour that we work. So if productivity rises, businesses can pay higher wages, they can make more profit without simply just putting up prices. Right. Since 2019, US labor productivity has risen by materially above trend in Japan has moved significantly higher too. Whereas when you look at Australian data, it's essentially gone sideways since 2020. Now this is really important for us in our inflation because if we're paying people more but not producing as much, those higher costs eventually show up in lower profits and higher inflation. And this would explain to a certain degree the valuations that look they are looking frothy here in Australia.
